name: Teardrop Glass Locket Necklace

specs.material: Gold plated brass with a glass front

description:
The teardrop hangs point-down and stays that way instead of spinning to show its back, which matters more on a locket than on any other pendant. This gold-plated locket necklace has a clear glass front and a hinged case, so it opens, takes whatever you want to carry in it, and closes again. Tiny charms, or a folded note trimmed down small. What goes in is yours to decide.

The case is gold-plated brass with a domed glass window, hung on a fine rolo chain that fastens with a lobster clasp. It is light enough to forget about by mid-morning, and the chain is fine enough to layer under a heavier necklace without crowding it.

Because the front is glass and the metal is plated rather than solid, treat it like the fashion piece it is. Keep it out of the shower, and wipe the window with a dry cloth when it fogs from moisture or perfume.

It works as a gift when you do not know someone's taste in jewellery but you do know their story. Fill it before you hand it over, or leave it empty and let them.

name: Heart Floating Locket with Birthstone Charms

specs.material: Gold plated brass with crystal charms

description:
Twelve charms arrive in the box, one for each month, so this gold-plated locket necklace can hold a single birthday or a whole household depending on how you fill it. The frame is an open heart with a glass face, and the charms sit loose inside it and shift as you move.

A note on what the charms actually are. They are coloured crystal cut to stand in for birthstones, not mined stones, and at this price nothing else would be true. What they do give you is the right colour for the right month, clear enough to read against the gold-tone backing.

The chain is a satellite style, so small beads punctuate the links and catch light along the length rather than only at the pendant. It fastens with a lobster clasp. The heart is light for its size, which keeps it sitting where you put it instead of sliding to one side through the day.

Mothers and grandmothers tend to like this one, and so does anyone who keeps track of family birthdays. Load one charm per child and add your own, and there is room left for later. Keep it away from perfume and take it off before a bath, since the plating and the glass both do better dry.

Reload it when the family grows. That is the part people forget a locket can do.

name: Heart Crystal Adjustable Ring
description:
Crystal and cubic zirconia behave differently under light, and this adjustable ring uses crystal. The heart is cut with broad flats rather than the tight brilliant faceting of a CZ, so it throws fewer sparks and more clean white flashes. Under a ceiling light it reads bright. In daylight it goes almost watery.

The setting is gold-plated stainless steel, polished up around the stone in a plain frame that keeps attention on the heart. Stainless steel underneath matters more than it sounds on a ring, since rings take more knocks than any other piece in a jewellery box. The band is open at the back and adjusts with light finger pressure, which covers most hand sizes without a size chart.

This sits at the top of the range, and the money is visible in the stone size and the finish rather than in any precious metal. Nothing here is solid gold and the copy will not pretend otherwise. The result is a large, well-cut clear heart on a base that will not rust if it meets water.

It suits a plain hand. One ring, nothing else on that finger, worn with a kurta or with jeans on a day you want one bright thing.

Take it off before you adjust it rather than bending it on the finger. Open bands loosen faster when they are reshaped while worn.

name: Silver-Tone Initial Signet Ring
description:
Signet rings started as a way to stamp wax, and the flat face never lost its appeal even after the sealing stopped. This one is a personalised silver-tone signet ring with a marquise face, narrow and pointed rather than the wide oval most signets take.

The letter is engraved into the face rather than printed on, so it holds up to the rubbing a ring gets from pockets and door handles. The band is fine, closer to a stacking ring than a chunky signet, which keeps the whole thing quiet on the hand.

About the colour. It is rhodium-plated brass, and rhodium is what gives the bright white finish. There is no silver in this ring despite the name, and that is worth saying plainly. Rhodium holds its brightness well for a plated piece as long as it stays clear of hand sanitiser and cleaning liquids.

A marquise face is a good shape for a single letter. It gives the engraver a long axis to work along, so letters with tails sit better than they do in a circle. Wear it on the little finger where signets traditionally sat, or on the index if you want it read.

name: Floating Locket Pendant

specs.material: Gold plated brass with a glass front

description:
Oval, heart, rectangle or round. The shape you pick changes this floating locket pendant more than you would expect, because each one frames its contents differently. The rectangle holds a straight line of charms. The round one lets them tumble.

All four are gold-plated brass with a clear glass front, opening at the back to be filled and closed again. The chain is a rolo, evenly linked and fine, with a lobster clasp. Nothing about the construction is heavy, which is deliberate on a locket meant to be worn most days rather than kept for occasions.

Filling it is the part people enjoy. Some put in loose charms. Others go with a chip of dried flower or a milk tooth, and because the case opens rather than seals, the contents change whenever the reason changes.

Plated brass over a glass face does not like heat or humidity, so a closed drawer beats a bathroom shelf.

A locket is one of the few pieces of jewellery that means nothing until someone fills it. That is either a drawback or the entire appeal.

name: Hug Embrace Open Ring
description:
Two hands, one coming from each side of the band, meeting in a hug where a stone would normally sit. That is the entire design of this gold-plated open ring, and it is enough.

The hands are sculpted with visible fingers and a slight overlap where they meet, so the piece reads as what it is even at arm's length. Cast in stainless steel and plated in gold tone, it carries more weight than the price suggests, which is usually a good sign on a plated piece.

The band is open at the back and adjusts by hand, so it fits a range of fingers and can move between them on days when fingers swell. Being open also keeps the hug sitting on top rather than rotating to the side, since a cuff grips where a closed band spins.

It reads as a friendship piece more than a romantic one. People buy two of these, one for themselves and one for the sister or the friend who got them through the year, and the meaning holds without any engraving.

Stainless steel underneath is the practical part. It will not rust if it gets wet, so the plating is the only thing needing care. Keep it off during dishes and it stays warm gold rather than going patchy at the high points where the hands meet.

The idea is obvious. It still works.

name: Silver-Tone Bow Twist Ring
description:
The band is the part worth looking at. It is twisted like a fine rope along its whole length, so the silver-tone finish catches light in a broken line instead of a flat shine, and the small cubic zirconia bow sits on top of that movement rather than on a plain surface.

The bow itself is modest, two loops set with clear stones, sized to sit inside the width of the finger rather than spilling over it. Rhodium plating over brass gives the bright white colour. Rhodium, not silver, which is the honest word for it.

Adjustable at the back, so it goes on any finger and comes off easily at the end of the day. That flexibility is useful on a ring this fine, because thin bands are the ones most likely to be wrong by half a size.

Bows have been quietly everywhere in Indian fashion jewellery for a couple of years now, and the twisted band keeps this version from looking like every other one. Wear it alone on a bare hand, or stack it against a plain band so the twist has something smooth to contrast with.

Cubic zirconia keeps the sparkle affordable and holds its clarity better than glass over time. It comes off before a hand wash and goes back on after. Thin plating and running water are not friends.

name: Watch Dial Ring

specs.type: Decorative watch dial, not a working timepiece

description:
It does not tell the time. The hands are painted in place and they stay where they are, which is the first thing to say about a watch ring before anything else about it.

What it is instead is a small piece of stainless steel jewellery shaped like a wristwatch and shrunk to fit a finger. The dial is black with a fine bezel, and the band is built from bracelet links so it looks like a watch strap wrapping the finger rather than a plain ring pretending to be one. Up close the link detail is what sells it.

Stainless steel means it holds its colour without plating to wear off, which is unusual at this price and worth knowing. It will not go green on the finger and it does not mind water. It also sits flat enough to go under a sleeve without catching.

The appeal is the joke and the craft at once. People notice it, then look closer at the links. Wear it on the index finger where it reads clearest, and keep the rest of that hand plain so it does not have to compete.

name: Mini Watch Ring

specs.type: Decorative watch dial, not a working timepiece

description:
Everything on this one is scaled down twice. It is a wristwatch reduced to ring size, and then the dial is reduced again inside that, which leaves a pearl-white face barely wider than a grain of rice.

The band is a woven link rather than a solid one, so it has the flex and texture of a real bracelet strap. It comes in silver or golden, both stainless steel, and the two read quite differently. Silver goes almost technical. Golden goes softer and sits closer to the rest of a jewellery box.

Like the larger watch ring in the range, the dial is decorative. The hands do not move. Saying so up front saves a disappointed unboxing, and anyone buying a ring this small is buying the look of a watch rather than the use of one.

Stainless steel is the quiet advantage. No plating to thin out, and no green marks after a wet day. That is rarer than it should be at this price.

Golden if it is joining a stack. Silver if it is doing its own thing.

name: Love Knot Ring
description:
One fine wire, tied once, and nothing else on the band. The love knot is one of the oldest ideas in jewellery and this gold-plated ring keeps it at its plainest, with no stones and no pavé edging to explain what the shape already says.

The knot sits slightly proud of the band so it catches light on the curve while the rest of the ring stays flat and quiet. It is a small design, sized to read on the hand without announcing itself from across a room. Stainless steel under the plating gives it more rigidity than a brass ring of the same thinness, which matters on a knot, because a softer metal would flatten the loop within a month.

Knots carry meaning without needing a word engraved on them, which makes this an easy gift when you want to say something and not overdo it. It also stacks well, since the flat band leaves room for a second ring beside it.

Plated gold over steel keeps its colour longest when it stays away from perfume and soap. Put it on after getting ready rather than before.

There is no stone to lose and no clasp to fail. Some pieces are easy to own and this is one.

name: Clear Heart Statement Ring
description:
Size is the whole argument. The faceted heart on this gold-plated ring is oversized on purpose, wide enough to cover most of the finger between knuckles, and the scalloped setting around it adds another ring of edges to catch light.

The stone is clear crystal, cut with flat planes that flash white rather than throwing colour the way a brilliant cut does. The scalloping is where the piece earns its price. Each small arc around the bezel picks up light separately from the stone, so the setting stays bright even when the heart is angled away from a lamp.

It is built on stainless steel with gold plating over it, and the band is open at the back with enough give to adjust across a couple of sizes. A ring this large needs that adjustment. It has to sit dead centre on the finger or the shape looks wrong, and an open band lets you correct it after you put it on.

Wear it with a plain outfit and nothing else on that hand. Big fashion rings work by being the only thing happening, and they stop working the moment a second ring joins them.

Keep it out of water and away from perfume and the plating stays even around the scallops, which are the first place a big setting goes dull.

Not a subtle ring. It was never meant to be.

name: Pink Baguette Stacking Ring
description:
Run a thumb along the band and the texture is the first thing you notice. This rose gold-plated stacking ring has a hand-worked surface rather than a polished one, so it holds light in small broken patches, and the single pink cubic zirconia baguette set across it sits flush against that roughness.

A baguette is a long rectangular cut, and set crossways like this it makes the ring read wider than its actual band. That is the trick of a good stacking ring. It has presence without bulk, so two or three can share a finger without the hand looking crowded.

Rose gold plating over brass gives the warm copper-pink colour, and it happens to flatter the stone. Pink on pink could go flat, but the CZ is a cooler pink than the metal, so the two separate rather than blur. Rose gold is also the finish that shows wear soonest on any fashion ring, since the copper tone thins to yellow before it goes silver. Off during hand wash buys it a long time.

It stacks best with plain bands. Put it beside something smooth and the texture reads as deliberate instead of accidental.

It is the ring people buy a second of, once they see how it sits next to a plain band.

name: Emerald-Green Baguette Stacking Ring
description:
The word emerald in the name is doing colour work, not material work. The stone is green cubic zirconia cut as a baguette, and that is worth saying in the first line rather than the last.

What the green does have is depth. It reads as a proper forest green rather than the bright bottle green cheap stones usually land on, and against warm gold plating that darkness is what makes the ring look more expensive than it is. The band is finely textured, not polished, so the metal stays matte while the stone stays glassy.

Slim is the point. This gold-plated stacking ring is narrow enough to wear three at a time, and green is one of the easier colours to repeat down a finger without it turning into a costume.

Green also has a specific advantage in Indian wear. It sits with almost every traditional colour and it does not fight with mehendi, which is more than can be said for a clear stone in the same season.

Brass under gold plating wants to stay dry. Wipe it after a warm day and keep it out of a humid bathroom drawer, and the texture stays crisp instead of clogging with residue.

name: Red Solitaire Thread Ring
description:
Garnet red is harder to get right than it looks. Too orange and it looks cheap. Too blue and it turns purple. This bezel-set stone lands in the deep middle, where the red still has some brown in it.

The band is the thinnest thing in the range. A hair-fine gold-plated thread ring with one small stone bezelled into it, which means the stone is held in a collar of metal rather than by claws. Bezels do not snag on clothing and they do not lose stones the way small prongs eventually do. The stone is cubic zirconia rather than any gemstone, and at this size the difference is invisible on the hand.

Red is the festive one of this set of four. It sits with red and maroon bangles without competing, and it holds its own against gold bangles on the same wrist, which a paler stone would not.

Thin rings like this are made to be worn in numbers. Two on one finger, or one each on three fingers, and the effect is deliberate rather than cluttered.

Stainless steel under the plating is why a band this thin does not bend out of round. That is the part you cannot see and the part that decides how long it lasts.

name: Pink Solitaire Thread Ring
description:
Some rings you notice all day. This is not one of them. The band is hair-fine gold-plated steel and the pink cubic zirconia set into it is small enough that the ring registers as a glint rather than an object, which is exactly what a lot of people want on a working day.

Soft pink is the gentlest stone in this group of four. It reads almost neutral in daylight and only shows its colour up close, so it goes to an office without argument and to dinner without changing.

The stone is bezel-set, sunk into a collar of metal so nothing stands proud of the band. That flatness is practical. It slides under a sleeve and it will not catch on a dupatta.

It also layers under a watch without adding bulk at the wrist end of the hand. Fine rings and a watch strap sit well together because neither is asking for attention.

Plated gold over stainless steel is a good combination on something worn daily. The steel keeps the shape, and the plating only needs to stay clear of soap and sanitiser to hold its warmth.

name: Clear Solitaire Thread Ring
description:
From two feet away this reads as a diamond solitaire, and there is no harm in that as long as everyone knows what it actually is. The stone is clear cubic zirconia, bezel-set into a hair-fine gold-plated band, and it does the job a small diamond would do at a tiny fraction of the cost.

Cubic zirconia is not a fake diamond so much as a different stone that happens to be clear and hard. It cuts cleanly and holds its polish, and up close it throws slightly more rainbow than a diamond does. That last bit is the tell, and it only shows if someone is looking for it.

Clear is the most useful of the four thread rings because it goes with the other three. Wear it beside the pink one or the green one and it acts as a spacer, which is how thin rings are meant to work together.

The bezel setting is the reason a stone this small survives daily wear. Nothing sticks up to catch, and the ring keeps a smooth profile against the finger next to it.

Hand cream is the enemy here, more than water. It collects around a bezel and dulls the stone, and a dry cloth once a week keeps a clear stone actually clear.

name: Green Solitaire Thread Ring
description:
Olive is an unusual choice for a small stone and that is the reason to pick it. Most green fashion stones go for emerald brightness. This one is duller and warmer, closer to the green of an old bottle held up to a window, and it looks better on brown skin for exactly that reason.

The setting is the same hair-fine gold-plated thread ring as the rest of this group, with a single bezel-set cubic zirconia sunk flush into the band. Nothing else, and nothing to catch. Keep perfume off it and the gold stays warm instead of thinning at the shoulders of the band.

Olive green pairs with mustard and rust, and generally with the warm side of the Indian wardrobe rather than the cool side. It also works with plain khaki cotton on an ordinary day, which is a strange thing to be able to say about a ring with a stone in it.

Because it is the least obvious of the four, it is the one most likely to be worn alone. A single fine ring on an otherwise bare hand reads as a decision rather than an accessory.

It is the one in this set that gets asked about. The other three get noticed and left alone.

name: CZ Bow Adjustable Ring
description:
A trillion cut is triangular, and two of them set base to base give you a bow without a single piece of metal shaped like one. That is the neat part of this silver-tone bow ring. The shape comes entirely from the stones.

Small pavé stones run along the edges of both triangles and down onto the shoulders of the band, so light travels across the whole width instead of sitting in two bright points. The finish is rhodium plating over brass, which is where the bright white comes from. No silver in it, whatever the colour suggests.

The band opens at the back and adjusts by hand, which is useful on a ring where the top is wide. A wide face wants to be centred, and an adjustable band lets you fix that after the ring is on rather than living with it.

Cubic zirconia is the right stone at this price. It stays clear where glass clouds, and it takes a proper facet, so a small bow like this keeps flashing after months of wear rather than going grey.

It reads as evening jewellery but works in daylight because the scale is small. That combination is rarer than it sounds on anything sparkly.

name: Gold Ribbon Bow Ring
description:
Nothing is set into this one. The bow is sculpted out of the metal itself and polished smooth, so the ring depends entirely on shape and shine rather than on any stone doing the work.

That turns out to be an advantage. Stones are what fail first on inexpensive rings, either falling out of small prongs or clouding until they look like plastic. A gold-plated ribbon bow ring with no settings has neither problem. There is nothing to lose and nothing to go dull except the plating.

The bow has proper folds, with the loops sitting at slightly different angles the way a real ribbon knot does rather than lying flat and symmetrical. The band is open at the back and adjusts, so it moves between fingers and between hands.

It is the cheapest ring in the range and it does not look it, mostly because polished metal photographs and wears better than cheap sparkle. Wear it on its own, or use it as the plain piece in a stack of stone-set rings.

Stainless steel under the plating means the core is solid. Keep it off during hand wash and the gold holds its warmth for a long time.

It is plain, and plain is hard to get wrong.

name: Rainbow Baguette Eternity Ring
description:
The stones go all the way around. That is what makes it an eternity ring rather than a half band, and it is why this one keeps working when your hand turns, since there is no plain back to swing into view.

The baguettes are channel-set, which means they sit between two rails of metal with no prongs between them. Colours run in sequence around the band, from red through to violet, cut as small rectangles that meet edge to edge so the colour is continuous rather than dotted.

Channel setting is the practical reason to like it. Nothing catches on a dupatta, and small stones in a channel are much harder to lose than small stones in claws.

Rainbow bands are one of the few pieces of fashion jewellery that work equally well alone or under a stack. Alone, the colour is the whole outfit's accent. Under a plain gold band, it becomes a line of colour peeking out.

Cubic zirconia in this many colours would cost a fortune as real stones, and nobody buying this expects otherwise. What you should expect is that the colours stay clear rather than fading, which CZ manages and dyed glass does not.

description:
You hear this one before you see it. The ghungroo bells strung along the chain make a small sound when the wrist moves, which is not something most watches do and not something anyone expects from a watch at all.

The dial is a working quartz analogue, round and small, set between two meenakari discs painted in the enamel colours the craft is known for. Meenakari is enamel fired into metal, and here it puts real colour on either side of the dial so the piece reads as a bracelet first and a watch second. The chain fastens with a lobster clasp and carries an extension, so it fits a range of wrists without a jeweller.

The plating sits on an anti-tarnish base, which earns its keep on a wrist more than anywhere else. Wrists get sweat and humidity, and the edge of every washbasin, and an untreated plated strap usually shows it within one monsoon. This one holds its colour through that.

Wear it with a kurta on a working day, or with a saree when a plain watch would look out of place. The enamel is what lets it cross over.

Keep the dial away from a direct water stream. Enamel and plating both survive daily life, and neither enjoys a tap.

name: Multicolour CZ Cluster Studs
description:
Rose, mint, amber and clear, packed close enough that no single colour takes over. These gold-plated cluster studs mix marquise and trillion cuts in one small group, and the different shapes are what keep the cluster from reading as a plain flower.

They sit close to the ear. That is the practical detail worth knowing on a stud with this much going on, because a cluster that stands proud looks heavier than it is and catches on hair. This one stays flat, held on a push-back post.

The colours are pale rather than saturated, which is why the mix works. Four strong colours in one earring would fight. Four soft ones read as a single pastel shimmer from any distance, and only resolve into separate stones when someone is close.

Cubic zirconia in several colours is the sensible way to get this look. Coloured glass clouds and dulls, and real stones in four colours would be a different conversation entirely. These hold their clarity as long as they stay out of the shower.

Good with a plain kurta or a white shirt, on any day the outfit is quiet and the ear can do something. Small enough for a working day, bright enough for the evening after it.

name: Silver-Plated Pink Leaf Studs
description:
Two parts, stacked. A single round stone sits at the top, and below it an open leaf-shaped frame is filled with pink marquise stones and edged in tiny pavé, so the earring has a top and a body rather than being one flat shape.

The openwork is the reason it does not look cheap. Solid metal behind stones is what makes budget earrings read as budget. Cutting the frame open lets skin show through the leaf and gives the whole thing a lightness its size would not suggest.

Silver plating over brass gives the cool white finish, which suits the pink better than gold would. Warm metal pushes pink towards peach. Cool metal keeps it pink.

They fasten with push-backs, so they are for pierced ears, and they sit against the lobe rather than hanging from it. Worth knowing before you order.

Pink and silver works harder in the evening than during the day. Wear them with a pastel suit, or with black, where the pink is the only colour in play.

Keep them out of water. Silver plating on brass dulls faster than gold plating does, and a dry wipe after wear is the whole of the maintenance.

name: Silver-Plated Blue Floral Studs
description:
Blue is under-used in Indian fashion jewellery, which is odd, because it sits against almost every traditional colour without fighting the gold worn elsewhere on the body. These silver-plated blue studs are a straightforward way to fix that in a jewellery box heavy on red and green.

Deep blue rounds circle a square princess-cut centre, and the square is what stops the cluster reading as a flower. Geometry instead of petals. The blue goes navy in low light and brightens under a lamp, so the pair shifts with the room rather than holding one pitch all evening.

Silver plating over brass gives the cold white that suits blue. Gold would warm it and lose the depth. Against bright white metal the blue reads deeper than it actually is.

They are small, flat to the lobe, on push-back posts, so they last a long day without weight. Nothing hangs and nothing catches in a dupatta.

Cubic zirconia, not sapphire. At this price the clarity of a well-cut CZ is the honest win, and the blue holds where dyed glass would fade. One dry wipe before they go back in the box is enough. Skin oil is what takes the shine off plating, not time.

name: Gold-Plated Mint Green Floral Studs

specs.stone: Mint green and clear cubic zirconia

description:
Frosted stones are unusual at this price. The mint green in these gold-plated floral studs is not polished glassy clear the way most coloured cubic zirconia is. It has a soft, slightly milky surface closer to sea glass, and that is what keeps the mint from looking like mouthwash.

Clear trillion cuts alternate with the mint around a square-cut centre, so the earring has two textures happening at once. Bright and sharp next to soft and matte. The contrast is what gives a small stud some depth.

Mint and gold is a pairing that took a while to become normal and now looks obvious. The warmth of gold plating pulls the green towards yellow-green rather than blue-green, which is the more flattering direction for most skin tones here.

Push-back posts, flat against the lobe. These are day earrings more than evening ones, because the frosted finish does not throw light the way an all-clear cluster would. Put them with cotton or linen and the pale end of a summer wardrobe.

Gold plating over brass needs the care rather than the stones. Off before a bath, and a dry cloth after a humid day.

name: Gold-Plated Pink Flower Studs
description:
Six petals, not five and not eight, which is the count that makes a flower read as a flower rather than a starburst. Each one is a pale pink marquise stone, pointed at both ends, arranged around a single clear round at the centre.

The pink is pale enough to stay neutral. That sounds like faint praise and it is not. A saturated pink stud commits an outfit to pink, while this one sits somewhere near skin tone from a distance and only shows its colour when someone is close.

Fine gold-tone settings hold each petal separately with visible metal between them, which is how the flower keeps its shape instead of collapsing into a blob of pink. It is a small piece of construction most buyers will never notice and would immediately miss.

These are the pair to give someone who does not wear much jewellery. Push-back studs, small enough that there is nothing to learn, and a pale pink that suits almost everyone.

Cubic zirconia and gold plating over brass is the whole material list. Keep them dry and they hold. Perfume is the usual culprit behind a stud going dull at the edges.

name: Delicate Pink Petal Floral Earrings
description:
Some earrings come off at the end of the day and some stay in for a week. These are the second kind. Five soft pink petals in a milled silver-tone frame, small enough that they disappear under hair and reappear when it moves.

The milling is worth a look. The frame around the petals is finished with a fine beaded edge rather than left smooth, an old technique borrowed from traditional silverwork, and it catches light in a row of tiny points around the outside of the flower. It gives a plain shape a border without adding size.

Silver plating and pink is a cooler combination than gold and pink, and it works better with everyday clothes. Denim, or plain cotton on a working day. A gold version of this earring would look dressed up. This one does not.

They are push-back studs, so pierced ears only. A stud this small tends to stay level through a long day where a heavier one tilts forward.

Clear cubic zirconia at the centre does the work of a diamond at a distance. The pink petals are the same stone, coloured. Nothing else in it.

description:
A cat's-eye stone has a single line of light running across it that moves as the stone tilts, and that is what sits at the centre of these gold-plated halo studs. Square cut, milky rather than clear, with the light band crossing it.

Around it are two rings of pavé cubic zirconia, one inside the other, held on fine gold-tone bridges rather than a solid backing. Double halos are usually reserved for larger pieces. On a stud this size the second ring is what makes it read as considered rather than plain.

The contrast is the point. A milky stone next to bright pavé gives two kinds of light in one earring, soft and sharp, where most studs offer only one.

Push-backs, flat to the lobe, for pierced ears. The slightly higher price than the rest of the stud range shows up in the halo work, which takes more setting labour than a single cluster does.

One honest line. The spec calls the centre a milky cat's-eye stone and does not say what it is made from, so treat it as a cat's-eye effect rather than a natural gemstone. The effect is real and it does what it should when the light moves.

name: Silver-Plated Floral Teardrop Nath
description:
The teardrop swings. That is the difference between a nath that reads as a stud with a hoop attached and one with some life in it, and it is what you notice first when the head turns.

The hoop is pavé-set all the way along its curve, with a small flower at the base where the drop hangs. Silver-plated brass gives the bright white finish, with clear cubic zirconia doing the sparkle. Not silver, despite the name on the listing.

It fastens with a screw, so it is for a pierced nose. A screw fitting is the more secure of the two common options and it does not work loose through a night of dancing the way a push fit sometimes does. It also takes a moment longer to put in, which is a fair trade.

Naths photograph larger than they wear. This one is small on the face and clear in a photo, which is the right way round for a wedding or a mehendi day where most of the record is somebody's phone.

Silver plating over brass wants a dry cloth after wear. Nose jewellery meets more skin oil than anything else in a jewellery box, and that is what dulls plating, not age.

description:
Strip the colour out of a peacock nath and what is left is the shape, which turns out to be the more useful version. This one sets the whole bird in clear cubic zirconia, with a marquise at the base and a single pearl-look bead hanging below.

Colourless has a practical advantage that gets overlooked. A red or a green stone commits the piece to matching, so it comes out for the outfits it suits and stays in the box for the rest. An all-clear nath goes with every colour a lehenga or a saree can be.

The gold-plated setting is what carries the peacock shape, curving along the hoop with the tail picked out in small stones. The bead below is pearl-look rather than the sea-grown kind, and it hangs on a short link so it moves independently of the hoop.

Screw fastening, so a pierced nose is needed. Screws hold through a long function better than a press fit, which is why most bridal naths use them.

At this price the value sits in the shape and the setting work rather than the materials. That is a fair place for it to sit, on a piece worn a few times a year and photographed heavily each time.

name: Gold Minimalist Stone Nath
description:
Not every nath is trying to be the centre of a wedding photograph. This gold-plated nath is the quiet one in the range, a slim hoop set with small stones and a single pavé teardrop where the weight would normally be.

The hoop is an open pressure fit rather than a screw, which means it holds by the spring of the metal instead of threading through. That makes it quicker to put on and take off, and it is the fitting people usually prefer for a nath they intend to wear more than a few times a year.

Scale is the whole design decision here. Small stones, a small drop, and nothing spreading across the cheek, so it works with everyday clothes as easily as with festive ones. A first nath is often this one, because it is the version that does not feel like a costume.

Gold plating over brass keeps the warm tone. Wipe it after wear and keep it away from face cream and perfume, both of which sit on the skin right where a nath lives.

There is a case for owning a nath you can wear on a Tuesday. This is that piece.

name: Silver-Plated Floral Cluster Nath
description:
The hoop stops being a hoop about halfway round. It opens into a spray of marquise stones set like petals, and a pavé teardrop hangs from the underside of that cluster, so the piece has a plain side and a busy side.

That asymmetry is the reason to pick this one. Worn so the cluster spreads towards the cheek, the plain curve sits inward, which reads better in a three-quarter photograph than a symmetrical design does.

Silver-plated brass gives the white metal colour, with clear cubic zirconia throughout. There is no silver in it, which the listing name does not make obvious, so it is worth saying here.

It fastens with a screw, so a pierced nose is needed. This is the most clearly bridal of the naths in the range, priced within reach of a piece that might only come out for a few functions.

Cluster naths hide their weight well. Marquise stones are long and light, so a spray of them looks like more metal than it is, and the piece does not drag at the piercing through a full evening.

name: Orange Enamel Floral Kada

specs.material: Anti-tarnish gold plated brass with enamel

description:
Orange is a difficult colour to wear and an easy one to want. This enamel kada solves the problem by keeping the orange warm rather than bright, closer to marigold than to traffic cone, with gold-tone flowers and trailing leaves raised across the dome of the bangle.

A kada is solid rather than hinged, so it goes over the hand in one movement and then stays put. That solidity is most of the appeal. It does not shift up the forearm through the day and it has no clasp to fail.

The enamel sits between the raised metal, which is the traditional way of doing it and also the practical way. Recessed enamel is protected by the metal around it, so the colour does not get scraped by a desk edge or a bag strap.

Anti-tarnish plating matters here more than on a piece worn occasionally. A kada takes constant contact and the raised flowers take the worst of it. On ordinary plated brass those high points go coppery within months. This one holds its gold tone through that contact with a wipe now and then.

Wear it alone against a plain sleeve, or with the marigold end of a festive wardrobe where the orange has company.

name: Pink Flower Bracelet

specs.closure: Lobster clasp with an extension chain

description:
The design runs along the chain rather than sitting on it. A gold-tone vine of leaves winds the length of the bracelet with small pink blooms opening along it and one larger flower at the centre, so the piece has a direction and a middle instead of a repeating pattern.

That matters on the wrist. A bracelet with a clear centre sits properly on top of the wrist and the eye finds it straight away, where an even pattern just reads as a band.

It fastens with a lobster clasp and carries an extension chain, so it adjusts across a range of wrist sizes without a fitting. Fine chain, light on the arm, comfortable under a sleeve.

The anti-tarnish base is the practical reason to choose this over a cheaper flower bracelet. Pieces like this get worn for a wedding and then sit in a drawer for four months, and ordinary plating comes out of that drawer dull. This one comes out looking the way it went in, which is most of what the extra money buys.

The stones are pink cubic zirconia, small and evenly matched. No pretence of anything else.

Pair it with a plain kurta where the pink can be the only colour, or with a pastel outfit it can echo.

name: Multicolour Tulip Bracelet
description:
Red, blue, green and violet, set in a run along a waved gold-tone bar chain, which is a lot of colour for a bracelet to carry without looking like a child's beads. It works because the stones are small and the gaps between them are wide.

The chain is doing the quiet work. Bar links waved rather than straight give the bracelet a soft ripple along its length, so it lies against the curve of the wrist instead of sitting on it like a rigid line.

It closes with a box clasp, the flat push-in kind rather than a lobster, and it sits neater against the skin. Box clasps are also easier to fasten one-handed once you have done it a few times.

Anti-tarnish plating earns its place around the settings. On a stone-set bracelet the metal between and beneath the stones is always the first area to grey, because it is the hardest part to reach with a cloth. This base resists that, so the bracelet keeps a consistent colour rather than going patchy around the brightest bits.

The stones are cubic zirconia in four colours. At this price that is the only honest way to have four colours at once, and it takes a red outfit or a blue one without ever having to match exactly.

Four colours on one wrist ought to be too much. Somehow it is not.

name: Pink Tulip Bracelet
description:
With only one colour to work with, the interest has to come from the cutting. Ovals and marquises alternate along this gold-plated tulip bracelet, rounded next to pointed, so the light behaves differently every few centimetres even though the pink never changes.

Single-colour bracelets are the ones that get worn most. There is no matching to think about and no clash to avoid, and a soft pink like this sits near neutral against most Indian skin tones.

The waved bar chain gives it flex without any obvious links, so it follows the wrist rather than standing away from it. A box clasp closes it flat.

Anti-tarnish plating is the difference between a bracelet that still looks new in the second year and one that does not. Plated brass without that base tends to go dull first at the underside, where the wrist rests against a desk all day. This one keeps its colour there too, which is the part nobody photographs and everybody sees.

Two things it does not have. There is no extension chain, so length matters, and there is no precious metal in it at any point.

Wear it with white, or on its own against bare skin in summer.

name: Blue Tulip Bracelet
description:
Blue stones with green ones set between them is the arrangement here, and the green is doing the job of leaves rather than competing as a second colour. Deep blue ovals carry the length of the waved gold-tone chain, with marquise greens angled between them like a stem line.

Blue and green together used to be a pairing people avoided. It reads as natural now, mostly because it is what actually happens in a garden, and against warm gold plating the two cool colours have something to push against.

This is the darkest of the three tulip bracelets, which makes it the evening one. Deep blue disappears in low light and then catches sharply under a lamp, so it does more in a lit room than a pale stone does.

The box clasp is where anti-tarnish plating pays off. Fingers find the clasp every time it goes on and comes off, and skin oil at that one spot is what turns ordinary plating coppery while the rest of the chain still looks fine. This base holds through that handling.

Cubic zirconia in blue and green, gold-plated brass beneath. Nothing sapphire, nothing emerald, and the listing does not claim otherwise.

Four bangles or eight, and the choice changes the piece more than the price does. Four sit quietly on one wrist. Eight fill the forearm and turn the ghungroo bells from an occasional sound into a constant one.

These are fine gold-plated bangles with clusters of tiny bells hung along them, in the style Kashmiri work is known for. The bells are the whole design. The bangle itself is deliberately plain so nothing competes with the movement.

Ghungroo bangles do something no other jewellery does, which is announce a person before she arrives. That is either the appeal or the reason to buy four instead of eight, depending on the wearer and the room.

Sizes run 2.4, 2.6 and 2.8, chosen over WhatsApp rather than on the page, so the size conversation happens with a person. Worth using rather than guessing, because bangle sizing is unforgiving and a set that will not clear the hand is a set that stays in the box.

Gold plating over brass, so keep them dry and store them away from damp. Bells collect moisture in their seams more than plain metal does.

Wear them with a plain sleeve where the sound has room, or stack them against solid bangles for contrast.

description:
Green bangles carry more meaning in India than most jewellery does. They come out for Teej, and in several communities they are what a newly married woman wears by default. Sixteen of them in deep lacquered green is not a small decision.

The set is glass rather than metal, lacquered to hold the colour, with gold and bronze beadwork dusted across the surface and clusters of ghungroo bells hung from some of the bangles. Glass gives a depth of colour that plated metal cannot. Light passes into it rather than bouncing off.

Glass also breaks. That is the honest trade and there is no way around it. A set of sixteen assumes some attrition over the years, which is part of why they are sold in sixteens and priced the way they are.

They sound different from metal bangles too. Glass on glass is a higher, drier clink, and sixteen of them make a lot of it.

Store them in a soft cloth rather than loose in a box, and keep them out of a hot car, since lacquer and heat do not get along.

name: Silver-Plated Snake Chain Ball Anklet
description:

The chain is a silver-plated snake link, the flat closely-wound kind that moves like a single piece of metal, and that is the right choice for an ankle. It lies flat against the skin and does not twist into itself, and there are no gaps for a chappal strap to catch.

Each one carries two small ball beads with a fine texture cut into them, spaced apart so they sit either side of the ankle bone.

Silver-plated brass gives the white metal colour at a price that makes a pair sensible rather than precious. Payal at this price is meant to be worn daily and replaced when it wears, and that is a reasonable way to own one.

Feet meet water more than hands do, which is the main thing to know. Plating on an anklet has a harder life than plating anywhere else, and taking them off before a bath adds months.

description:
Nazar beads have been made in more or less this shape for a very long time, and the reasoning behind them has never needed explaining in India. Two of them sit on this black bead anklet, blue and white against a strand of faceted black glass, with a small silver-tone spiral charm hanging alongside.

The beads are glass, faceted rather than smooth, so they catch light in small hard points as the foot moves. Black is an unusual colour for an anklet and a useful one. It reads as jewellery rather than as tradition, and it goes with clothes a plain silver payal would look odd against.

Two anklets come in the set. A lobster clasp with an extension chain closes each one, so they adjust across a range of ankle sizes rather than needing to be exact.

The findings are silver-plated, which is the part that needs looking after. Glass beads are indifferent to water. Plated clasps and charms are not, so these come off before a bath like everything else in the box.

The question of whether it works is not one a product page can settle. What it does do is put a bit of blue at the ankle, which has been reason enough for a long time.

A cable chain is the simple round-link kind, fine enough here to stay flat against the ankle bone rather than sitting proud. It closes with a lobster clasp and an extension chain, so the length adjusts without a jeweller.

description:
Organza and satin behave differently and this clip uses both. The bow is organza, the stiffer, slightly transparent fabric that holds a loop without drooping, and the two tulips trailing from the knot are satin, soft and shiny, on green ribbon stems.

That difference is why the bow keeps its shape all day. A satin bow collapses by afternoon. An organza one stands up to being sat against a chair back and pushed around by a dupatta.

It fixes with a metal alligator clip, the sprung kind with teeth, which grips fine hair better than a snap clip does. The tulips hang below the knot and move when the head does.

At this price it is close to an impulse buy, and it is the kind of thing that ends up in a handbag and eventually in somebody else's hair.

It is fabric, so keep it dry and press the bow flat under a book if it gets crushed in a bag.

The clip is metal and firm, which a bow this size needs. A large satin bow on a weak clip slides down the hair within an hour.

It suits long hair worn down or a low ponytail, where the tails have somewhere to fall. On short hair the tails are the wrong length for the head.

name: Pear-Petal CZ Flower Ring

specs.material: Rose gold plating (base metal not stated in source)
specs.care: Keep away from water and perfume; store in a dry place when not in use

description:
Five petals, one round stone in the middle. Each petal is a pear-cut stone laid over a bed of smaller rounds, and together they make up the whole face of this rose gold flower ring, since the band behind the flower stays slim and plain.

The stones are cubic zirconia, the clear sparkle half the market lists as American Diamond, and the pear cuts do most of the work. A pear has a point and a belly, so each petal returns light at a slightly different angle as your finger moves, which keeps a small flower lively without any single big stone. The warm rose tone of the plating holds the five settings close, and the flower reads as one bloom rather than five parts.

The band is open at the back and adjusts with a gentle squeeze, so it fits most fingers without a size chart. Worn often it behaves itself, though the plating will thank you for a wipe after wear and a spot in the box away from perfume sprays.

Flower rings tend to read younger the bigger they get. This one stays at the small end, closer in spirit to a stud earring than to a cocktail piece, which is why it earns its keep on an ordinary weekday hand and still holds up at a party.

name: Butterfly Wing Bypass Ring

specs.material: Rose gold plating (base metal not stated in source)

description:
The two wings do not match. That is the design of this butterfly bypass ring: one wing is set edge to edge with small cubic zirconia, the other is a smooth panel with a soft pink, shell-look finish that returns light as a sheen rather than a sparkle. A single round stone sits where the wings meet.

The open bypass band is the other half of the idea. The wings approach from opposite sides and pass each other across the top of the finger instead of joining, so the gap between the ends is both the fit and the picture: ease them apart or press them closer and the ring sizes itself, while the butterfly keeps its mid-flight look.

On the hand it sits low and small. The worn photographs show it honestly, one wing of sparkle and one of colour on a slim rose gold-plated band, a ring that reads as detail rather than centrepiece. Flat-set designs like this slide under gloves and sleeves without complaint, which claw-set rings rarely manage.

A note on the pink, since it matters: it is a finish, not a stone, and it is why this piece photographs warmer than an all-clear setting would. If most of your jewellery leans plain, one small wing of colour is an easy place to start.

name: Oval CZ Swirl Cocktail Ring

specs.material: Rose gold plating (base metal not stated in source)

description:
Ninety-nine rupees is doing a lot of work here. The centre stone is a full oval cubic zirconia, big enough to read from across a room, and the setting swirls two curved lines of smaller stones past it, so the whole face of this oval CZ cocktail ring moves when your hand does.

A swirl halo is a different animal from a neat border. The curves run past the oval rather than around it, which gives the design a direction, almost a rotation, and stops it sitting as a static lozenge on the finger. Between the curves the rose gold plating shows through in warm channels, so there is metal in the picture as well as sparkle.

It has the scale of the rings that usually come out for receptions and festive dinners, and the adjustable open band means it can move between hands, which big rings are often asked to do. It needs no supporting jewellery.

Big stones at small prices are exactly where honesty matters most, so, plainly: this is cubic zirconia over plated metal, sold as that. What the money buys is cut and scale. Keep it dry, give it the odd wipe, and the shine it left the box with is the shine it keeps.

name: Lattice Criss-Cross CZ Ring

specs.material: Rose gold plating (base metal not stated in source)
specs.care: Keep away from water and perfume; store in a dry place when not in use

description:
Two bands cross once and go their separate ways. That is the whole architecture of this criss-cross rose gold ring: one strand carries a line of small cubic zirconia, the other stays plain polished metal and widens at each end into a leaf-shaped tip pierced with rows of tiny openwork squares.

The cut-outs earn their keep. Openwork catches shadow the way stones catch light, so the pierced tips read as pattern even when nothing is sparkling, and the ring holds some interest in flat indoor light where pavé alone goes quiet. Less metal also means less weight, which your hand notices at the end of a long day rather than in the first minute.

The crossing point sits slightly off-centre and the open ends tuck under the finger, where they double as the adjustment. Ease them apart or press them in and the ring resizes without tools. Nothing about the shape demands an occasion; it wears as easily on a workday as a plain band does, with more to look at.

Perfume is the one enemy worth naming. Spray settles into openwork and dulls plating from inside the pattern outward, so this ring goes on after the scent, never before.

name: Beaded-Edge CZ Band Ring

specs.material: Rose gold plating (base metal not stated in source)

description:
Some rings apply for the loudest job on the hand. This CZ half eternity band takes the other one. A single row of round cubic zirconia sits in a channel across the top of the finger, and a fine beaded edge runs along both sides, an old jeweller's detail called milgrain that gives the metal a soft, slightly vintage grain up close.

A channel setting holds the stones between two continuous walls of metal rather than in individual claws. Nothing stands proud of the band, nothing snags on knitwear or a dupatta, and small stones held this way are far harder to lose than small stones in prongs. The sparkle stops at the shoulders; turn the ring and the plain rose gold-plated back shows instead, which is normal for a half eternity and part of why it stays comfortable.

This is the band that stacks under a bigger ring without arguing with it, and the one you can put on in the morning and forget by lunch. It asks nothing of an outfit and quietly improves most of them.

Store it dry between wears. Plating lasts longest when water never reaches it, and this design has no other demands to make.

specs.material: Rose gold plating (base metal not stated in source)

description:
There is real weight to this one, and the weight is the point. Three strands interlace across the top of the finger, two of them polished rose gold plate looping over and under each other, the third a crossover CZ band running through the middle, set edge to edge with small stones. Together they read as one wide woven surface rather than three thin ones.

Crossover bands flatter movement. Because the strands run at angles instead of straight around, light keeps finding a new polished face as the hand turns, and the pavé line returns part of that light as sparkle rather than shine. From arm's length the weave blurs into a single band with a bright seam through it.

Width changes how a ring wears. This one fills the base of the finger the way a kada fills a wrist, so it suits hands on which slim bands tend to disappear, and it carries a full outfit's worth of interest alone. Party wear is its natural habitat, though nothing about the construction objects to an ordinary Tuesday.

The open back adjusts to size. Give the polished strands their wipe after wear, since broad shiny surfaces show fingerprints sooner than textured ones do, and the band keeps looking deliberate rather than handled.

name: Open Heart and Teardrop CZ Ring

specs.material: Rose gold plating (base metal not stated in source)
specs.care: Keep away from water and perfume; store in a dry place when not in use

description:
Hearts on rings usually arrive solid and filled with stones. This one is drawn. On this open heart CZ ring an outline of small cubic zirconia traces the shape and leaves the middle empty, so your skin shows through and becomes part of the design. Across a small gap sits a single teardrop stone, its point turned towards the heart.

The open front does two jobs at once. It is the adjustment, since the ends ease apart or press together to fit, and it is the composition, because the space between heart and teardrop is what lets the design read as two clear thoughts instead of one crowded cluster.

An outlined heart is easier to live with than a solid one. It suggests the motif without shouting it, which keeps the ring wearable long after the occasion that prompted it has passed, and it photographs cleanly against skin, worth knowing if the ring is a gift and the giving will be photographed.

Gifting is where this piece most obviously belongs. A heart motif and a fit that never needs the recipient's ring size settle the two practical questions a surprise usually raises. The stones are cubic zirconia in rose gold-plated metal, stated plainly, so the gesture never has to carry an asterisk.

name: Fan-Shaped Crystal Pendant Necklace, Gold-Toned

specs.stone: Glass or cubic zirconia, unclear from text
specs.care instructions: Keep away from moisture and perfumes; store in a dry, safe place

description:
A fan shape gives a pendant more edges to catch light than a round or teardrop cut would, and this one uses that: a geometric fan-shaped drop set with small clear stones, hung on a gold-toned chain that keeps the rest of the design plain so the pendant does all the work. It's a bigger, more noticeable shape than a simple solitaire, without tipping into full statement-piece territory.

That middle ground makes it useful for more than one kind of outfit. It has enough presence for a going-out top or a festive kurta, but it's not so large that it looks out of place with an office collar on a day you want a bit more sparkle than usual. The chain sits at a length that lets the pendant fall just below the collarbone, where a geometric shape like this actually reads clearly instead of getting lost against the skin.

The stones are glass or cubic zirconia rather than genuine crystal or diamond, honestly labelled for what they are on a ₹110 pendant, and the chain is gold-toned rather than solid gold. Keep it away from moisture and perfume, and store it somewhere dry so the plating holds its finish. For the price, it's a reasonable way to add one geometric, slightly-more-dressed-up piece to a jewellery rotation that's mostly simpler daily pieces.
